question: A member services officer must explain a change to membership fees. The explanation goes to members of fifteen years and to people who joined last month. Which request is most likely to produce copy she can use?
options: A) Ask for two versions of the notice, stating what each group already knows about fees and what each has to do.
B) Ask for one notice aimed at long-standing members, since newer members will accept whatever the notice tells them.
C) Ask for one notice in neutral wording, and let each reader work out for themselves which parts of it apply to them.
D) Ask for a single notice, plus a glossary at the end explaining every term that appears in the fee schedule.
correct_answers: A) Ask for two versions of the notice, stating what each group already knows about fees and what each has to do.
explanations: Correct. Naming each audience and what it already knows lets the request specify different starting points and different required actions, which is what actually separates copy that lands from copy that has to be rewritten.
Writing for the group with the most history assumes background the newest members do not have, and it treats their confusion as acceptable rather than as a cost.
A notice that serves neither group well is the usual result: long-standing members wade through explanations they do not need, and new members meet references they cannot place.
A glossary bolts definitions onto the end without changing the body of the notice, so the parts that assume familiarity still assume it.
